projects.title: UWASIC
projects.summary: The functional-unit control module for Waterloo’s ray-tracing ASIC: SystemVerilog that decodes 11 micro-ops and dispatches them to the ALU, multiplier, and CORDIC units.
overview: I’m an RTL design member of UWASIC, the University of Waterloo’s chip design team, which is building a ray-tracing ASIC. I wrote the chip’s functional-unit control module in SystemVerilog. It sits between the micro-op channel and the three arithmetic units: the ALU, the multiplier, and the CORDIC unit.

For each micro-op, the module decides which unit should run it, collects its operands, hands the work over when that unit is ready, and writes the result back to the register file when the unit finishes. Before this, I completed UWASIC’s digital-design onboarding project, an SPI-controlled PWM peripheral.

sections.title: Decoding 11 micro-ops
body: Each micro-op is decoded into a target unit and, for units that run more than one operation, a 3-bit opcode for that unit.
bullets: ALU: add, subtract, equal, not equal, less than, and greater than or equal.
CORDIC: divide, square root, cosine, and magnitude.

sections.title: Operands
body: Operands normally come from the register file’s two read ports, addressed by the micro-op’s two source registers. Scalar macro-ops carry their operands on the micro-op channel instead, so a direct flag switches a mux between the register file and the channel. The operands, opcode, and format field go to all three units, but only the selected unit sees a valid request.

sections.title: Valid/ready handshakes
body: Each unit connects through the same SystemVerilog interface, with a valid/ready handshake on the request side and a done signal on the response side. The module passes the selected unit’s ready signal back up the micro-op channel, so a micro-op is accepted only in a cycle where it is valid and that unit is ready. In that cycle, the module also records the micro-op’s destination register for that unit, so the result is written to the right place when it arrives.

sections.title: Writing results back
body: When a unit finishes, the module writes its result to the destination register it recorded and signals on the micro-op channel that the operation is done. The register file has one write port, so writeback uses a fixed priority: the ALU first, then the multiplier, then the CORDIC unit.

outcome: The functional-unit control module is written, connecting the micro-op channel to all three arithmetic units. I’m now supporting the verification team as the module is tested and integrated into the chip’s RTL-to-GDS flow.

projects.title: UWAFT
projects.summary: A single-cell Li-ion battery monitor and relay load switch board, designed in Altium with an STC3100 gas gauge and an STM32.
overview: I’m on the electrical subteam of UWAFT, the University of Waterloo Alternative Fuels Team. For my electrical onboarding project, I designed a battery monitor and relay board in Altium Designer. It monitors a single Li-ion cell and can connect or disconnect a load.

An STC3100 gas gauge measures the battery’s voltage and current, sensing the current through a 30 mΩ shunt and counting the charge that flows in and out. An STM32F030 microcontroller reads the gauge over I2C and switches a relay to turn the load on or off.

sections.title: The circuit
body: The STM32 reads the gauge on I2C (PB6 and PB7, with 4.7 kΩ pull-ups) and drives the relay from PA8 through an AO3400A MOSFET on the low side of the coil, with a flyback diode across the coil. An MCP1700 LDO supplies 3.3 V, and the MCU runs on its internal 8 MHz oscillator, so the board needs no crystal.
bullets: Every VDD and VDDA pin has its own decoupling capacitor, and the LDO has input and output capacitors.
BOOT0 has a 10 kΩ pull-down, and NRST has a 100 nF filter capacitor.
A 2×4 debug header brings out SWD for programming, plus I2C, battery voltage, 3.3 V, and ground for testing.
Every part can be soldered by hand: 0805 passives and leaded packages, with no bottom-terminated parts.

sections.title: Layout
body: The board is 44 × 40 mm: 2-layer FR-4 with 1 oz copper and four M3 mounting holes. I laid it out to UWAFT’s 2-layer rule set (0.127 mm minimum clearance and trace width, 0.3/0.6 mm vias), and it passes DRC with zero violations.
bullets: The power path, from the battery through the relay to the load, runs on 1.2–1.5 mm traces; signals use 0.25 mm.
Solid ground pours fill both layers. Ground pads use thermal reliefs, except the high-current shunt-ground and load-return pads, which connect directly.
Almost all routing is on the top layer. Only two short traces, SWDIO and the header’s battery-voltage feed, run on the bottom.
The silkscreen marks polarity, the BATT and LOAD connectors, the header pins, and the board name and revision.

sections.title: Measuring across the shunt
body: The shunt is only 30 mΩ, so its voltage drop is small: 30 mV at 1 A. Even a little resistance in a shared ground trace would add a noticeable error to that measurement. The shunt is Kelvin-sensed: the gauge’s sense lines run straight to the shunt pads, and a cutout in the ground pour means ground meets the gauge only at the shunt. Several vias tie the shunt’s ground pad to the bottom plane.

outcome: Version 1.0 of the board is laid out and passes DRC with zero violations. It took me from schematic to a finished two-layer layout, including the details that matter on a measurement board: Kelvin sensing, solid ground, and wide traces for the high-current path.

projects.title: SPI-Controlled PWM Peripheral
projects.summary: A Verilog SPI Mode 0 peripheral with five registers and sixteen outputs that drives a 3 kHz PWM, tested with cocotb and taken to GDS through Tiny Tapeout.

cover.alt: Top-down view of the chip layout: rows of standard cells crossed by vertical power straps, with the routed SPI and PWM logic concentrated in the upper half.
cover.caption: GDS layout of the peripheral, shown in a 3D layout viewer.

overview: This was my digital-design onboarding project for UWASIC, Waterloo’s chip design team: a Verilog SPI Mode 0 peripheral that drives PWM outputs. It took one design from RTL, through automated simulation, to a generated chip layout.

sections.title: The peripheral
body: The peripheral has five registers and sixteen outputs, configured over SPI Mode 0. Two-stage clock-domain crossing (CDC) moves signals safely between clock domains.
bullets: Verilog RTL for the SPI interface and output controls.
A register interface for configuring the outputs and the PWM.
Two-stage CDC for signals crossing clock domains.

sections.title: Verification
body: I wrote Python/cocotb tests, simulated with Icarus Verilog, that check the 3 kHz PWM at 0%, 50%, and 100% duty cycle, along with the output-enable behavior.

sections.title: From RTL to GDS
body: I configured Tiny Tapeout and GitHub Actions to run the simulation tests and generate the GDS layout files automatically.

outcome: The peripheral is complete, with automated simulation tests and GDS generation. It gave me the foundation for the functional-unit control RTL I later wrote for UWASIC’s ray-tracing ASIC.

projects.title: SignEd
projects.summary: An interactive ASL learning website that connects live hand-pose recognition with guided lessons.

cover.alt: The five-person SignEd team standing in front of a projected slide that reads “1st Place Winner, Beginner Tier, $650, SignEd”, most of them making the ASL “I love you” sign.
cover.caption: Our team after SignEd won first place in the Beginner Tier at Hack the Bias.

overview: SignEd is an ASL learning website we built at Hack the Bias, a hackathon with 101 participants, where it won first place in the Beginner Tier. As the sole programmer on our five-person team, I developed the application using Python, Flask, JavaScript, and HTML/CSS, connecting computer vision to an interactive learning experience.

sections.title: Recognizing a sign
body: MediaPipe and OpenCV provide the hand-tracking pipeline. I normalized 21 three-dimensional hand landmarks by wrist position and hand size, then used distance-weighted K-nearest neighbors to recognize all 24 static letters of the ASL alphabet. J and Z are left out because they are signed with motion.

sections.title: Connecting recognition to learning
body: Live recognition feedback is connected to guided lessons. A learner unlocks progression after holding the correct sign for three seconds, connecting the recognition result to a clear practice goal.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Implemented the Python/Flask application and the browser interface.
Built the hand-landmark normalization and pose-classification pipeline.
Connected live feedback to lesson progression.

outcome: SignEd won first place in the Beginner Tier at Hack the Bias. The project brought together computer vision, a web interface, and guided practice in one ASL learning experience.

projects.title: VEX Robotics
projects.role: Built the intake, flywheel & catapult; programmed autonomous
projects.summary: A VEX competition robot: a flywheel design that qualified our team for the 2023 World Championship, then a catapult rebuild.

cover.alt: Team 2088D’s first robot on the floor: an aluminum VEX frame on omni wheels with a disc intake, a flywheel, and a red 2088D license plate.
cover.caption: Design 1: the flywheel robot that qualified our team for Worlds.

overview: I competed in VEX robotics on team 2088D from 2022 to 2024. In the 2022–23 season, we built two versions of our robot: a flywheel design that qualified us for the World Championship, and a catapult rebuild. I built the intake, the flywheel, and the catapult, and I programmed the autonomous routines.

sections.title: Design 1: the flywheel robot
body: Our first robot collected discs with an intake and launched them with a spinning flywheel. I built both, then tuned the flywheel speed and the intake spacing to make shots more consistent and reduce jams. This is the robot that placed second in Alberta Provincial Robot Skills and qualified us for Worlds.

sections.title: Autonomous routines
body: I programmed the robot’s autonomous routines: the code that drives it on its own at the start of each match and in programming skills runs.

sections.title: Design 2: the catapult rebuild
body: Even after tuning, the flywheel wasn’t as reliable as we wanted. After qualifying for Worlds, we rebuilt the robot around a catapult, which launches a whole stack of discs in one motion. I built the catapult.

images.alt: The rebuilt robot on a workbench, nearly finished: an aluminum frame on omni wheels with a geared catapult arm held back by rubber bands, and a practice field behind it.
images.caption: The catapult rebuild, nearly finished.

images.alt: Video of the catapult launching a stack of three discs into the goal.
images.caption: The catapult launching three discs into the goal.

outcome: The flywheel robot placed second in Alberta Provincial Robot Skills and qualified our team for the VEX Robotics World Championship, where we competed in Dallas in 2023. Its reliability problems led to the catapult rebuild.

projects.title: C++ Ray Tracer
projects.summary: A C++ path tracer built up in stages, from a first ray–sphere hit test to Monte Carlo diffuse lighting.

cover.alt: The ray tracer’s final render: a matte grey sphere resting on curved grey ground under a blue sky, with soft shading and a fine grain of sampling noise.
cover.caption: The final render: diffuse lighting averaged over many random samples per pixel.

overview: I built a path tracer from scratch in C++, following the approach in Ray Tracing in One Weekend. It sends rays from the camera through each pixel into the scene and works out what colour each one should be.

I built it up in four stages, each adding one idea and checked with a render before moving on: first finding what a ray hits, then the surface’s orientation, then a sky, and finally how light bounces.

sections.title: Stage 1: rays and a sphere
body: Each ray is a parametric line, P(t) = O + t·d. Substituting it into the sphere’s equation gives a quadratic in t: the discriminant says whether the ray misses, grazes, or hits the sphere, and the smallest positive root is the point the camera sees.
For the first render, rays that hit the sphere were coloured red and rays that missed were black.

images.alt: A flat red circle on a black background.
images.caption: Stage 1: the hit test. Red where a ray hits the sphere, black where it misses.

sections.title: Stage 2: surface normals
body: To make the sphere look three-dimensional, each hit point needs a surface normal. For a sphere it is the direction from the centre to the hit point, (P − C) / R. Before adding any lighting, I checked the normals visually by mapping their x, y, and z components from [−1, 1] to red, green, and blue.

images.alt: A sphere on a black background, shaded in a smooth gradient of cyan, blue, purple, and pink by the direction its surface faces.
images.caption: Stage 2: each pixel coloured by the direction of the surface normal.

sections.title: Stage 3: a sky
body: Next, I replaced the black background with a sky. Each ray that misses takes its colour from a linear blend between white and blue, based on how far up it points.

images.alt: The normal-coloured sphere against a sky that fades from light blue at the top to near-white at the bottom.
images.caption: Stage 3: a gradient sky behind the sphere.

sections.title: Stage 4: diffuse light and random sampling
body: Finally, I made the surfaces matte. When a ray hits one, it bounces off in a random direction and picks up colour from wherever it goes next. To choose the direction, I pick random points in a cube and keep the first one that falls inside a unit sphere. This is Monte Carlo path tracing.

With one random sample per pixel, the image was very noisy. Averaging many samples per pixel smooths out both the noise and the jagged edges, because the average converges to the true lighting as the number of samples grows. The cost is time: more samples meant much longer renders.

images.alt: A matte grey sphere resting on curved grey ground under a blue sky, with soft shading and a fine grain of sampling noise.
images.caption: Stage 4: matte surfaces lit by random bounces, averaged over many samples per pixel.

outcome: The finished ray tracer turns vectors, quadratic equations, and random sampling into soft, realistic shading. It is limited to matte spheres, with no specular reflections, transparency, or other shapes yet. Natural next steps are ray–plane intersections and triangle meshes, which would allow more complex scenes.

projects.title: Calgary Ace Learning Center
projects.summary: A student-run tutoring nonprofit that gives all of its proceeds to children’s healthcare: $5,335 so far for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation.

cover.alt: Six members of Calgary Ace Learning Center in front of the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation logo, holding a large cheque made out to the foundation for $5,335.
cover.caption: Presenting our cheque for $5,335 to the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation, December 2025.

highlights.label: Donated to the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation

overview: I co-founded Calgary Ace Learning Center (CALC), a nonprofit where IB and AP students tutor younger students. All of the proceeds from tutoring go to the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation.
I tutor, help run the organization, led our fundraising, and built our website.

sections.title: Teaching & volunteering
body: I have contributed more than 400 volunteer hours to tutoring and organizing. Teaching is the core of what we do: students who have been through demanding courses help younger students build the same skills.

sections.title: Giving it all to children’s healthcare
body: Every dollar from tutoring goes to the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation. On December 4, 2025, we presented the foundation with a cheque for $5,335, and we signed our names on a heart that is still on the wall there.

images.alt: A red paper heart on a painted green wall, signed “Calgary Ace Learning” with six names, including Lucas Wu, and a smiley face.
images.caption: The heart we signed, still on the wall.

sections.title: Building the website
body: I built CALC’s website in WordPress. It introduces our services and our team, shares updates on a bulletin page, and lets families book tutoring sessions.

images.alt: The Calgary Ace Learning Center home page: a pink banner reading “Get Ahead Today” and a Book button beside a photo of a tutoring session framed by hand-drawn math doodles, with Our Team, Bulletin, Home, and Book links above.
images.caption: The home page of the WordPress site I built.

outcome: An ongoing commitment to education and community service: more than 400 volunteer hours, and $5,335 donated to the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation so far.
